title: 24-hour mental health crisis team called for in wake of Mutch police shooting
article: Rhett Mutch had threatened to kill himself with a knife when police responded to his mother's home on Dallas Road in Victoria on Nov. 1, 2014.
Instead, the troubled 20-year-old died from a bullet to his neck, fired by one of the officers called there to help.

A Coroner's Jury wants the B.C. government to adequately fund a coordinated crisis team to be trained and in place around the clock in order to help ensure others going through an acute mental health event don't suffer a similar fate.
It is one of 12 recommendations a jury has made following an inquest this week into Mutch's death.

According to a media release issued late Friday by the BC Coroner's Service, the recommendations focus on police response for those in mental health crises, as well as expanding support for youth transitioning out of government care.
In the aftermath of testimony that kicked off Monday in B.C. Supreme Court in Victoria, the jury found that Mutch died as a result of a gunshot wound to the neck, and classified the death as suicide.

The jury's recommendations included a call to the Ministry of Health to provide adequate funding to the Integrated Mobile Crisis Response team program to be able to provide services 24 hours per day, seven days per week.

To the Ministry of Public Safety and Solicitor General, the jury recommended ensuring that online retraining for Crisis Intervention De-escalation is refreshed with new and relevant scenarios every two years. It also suggested consideration of a worn bodycam-style automatic audio and/or audiovisual device with GPS and timestamp to assist and supplement the review of radio and/or cell phone records of events.

To the Ministry of Children and Family Development, the jury urged fully supported transition plans from child, to youth, to young adult, to 19 plus. It also recommended that the Young Adult Program add a Life Skill Options component with an option to renew every three months up to age 25, and that continuation of the same support workers be maintained as a child ages.
To the South Island Police Departments, the recommendation was that all members be made aware of and encouraged to participate in care services after a critical incident.

To Prime BC and the Integrated Mobile Crisis Response Team, the jury urged that a memorandum of understanding be entered into so that a record of attendance at a residence or by a complainant by the Integrated Mobile Crisis Response team is noted and flagged in Prime.

To the Police Chiefs of Southern Vancouver Island and Island Health, the recommendation was that after a defined number of multiple crisis calls to police from a single source are received, an early intervention from appropriate ministries should be initiated and a collaborative safety plan created.

To the Independent Investigations Office and the BC Association of Police Chiefs, the jury recommended considering amendments to their memorandum of understanding to ensure that police officers can debrief in a timely manner.

To Prime BC, the Ministry of Health, and the Ministry of Children and Family Development, the recommendation was to enter into a memorandum of understanding to provide access to information between all three agencies.
Finally, to the Legal Aid Society of BC, the jury recommended providing a fee category for legal representation at a Coroners Inquest for the family of the deceased person.
Inquests are called to determine the facts surrounding a death. Juries may not find fault or blame but may make recommendations aimed at preventing future deaths in similar circumstances.
The Independent Investigations Office (IIO) of B.C. cleared a Victoria police officer of any wrongdoing in June of 2016.
Mutch's mother, Marney Mutch, has launched a wrongful death suit against the Victoria Police Department and the City of Victoria in connection with the incident.
